title: Abdominal Pain

correct_orders.rationale: Good screening. Can be gathered from DRE.

rationale.Physical Exam: Rectal: Could be source of symptoms — DRE.
rationale.CBC with differential: Leukocytosis supports infection. SIRS: WBC >12K + fever >100.4°F.
rationale.Urinalysis: GU pathology can present as abdominal pain.
rationale.Bacterial culture, blood: Meets SIRS criteria — blood cultures warranted.
rationale.Bacterial culture, urine: Abdominal pain + fever + elevated WBC — urine culture may determine cause.
rationale.Abdominal X-ray (acute series / AP): Good start. Rule out free air (perforation).
rationale.CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast: Gold standard for definitive diagnosis. Will show 2 cm abscess — complicated diverticulitis.
rationale.Occult blood, stool: Good screening. Can be gathered from DRE.
rationale.IV fluids (NS / LR / D5LR): Nausea and vomiting — IV fluids for hydration.
rationale.Diet, NPO: Bowel rest — essential in acute diverticulitis.
rationale.Ceftriaxone IV: Complicated diverticulitis: IV cefazolin/cefuroxime/ceftriaxone + metronidazole or ampicillin/sulbactam alone. Small abscess (<3-4 cm) = antibiotics alone, no drainage needed.
rationale.Metronidazole IV: Complicated diverticulitis: IV cefazolin/cefuroxime/ceftriaxone + metronidazole or ampicillin/sulbactam alone. Small abscess (<3-4 cm) = antibiotics alone, no drainage needed.
rationale.Pip-Tazo: Complicated diverticulitis: IV cefazolin/cefuroxime/ceftriaxone + metronidazole or ampicillin/sulbactam alone. Small abscess (<3-4 cm) = antibiotics alone, no drainage needed.
rationale.Ampicillin-Sulbactam: Complicated diverticulitis: IV cefazolin/cefuroxime/ceftriaxone + metronidazole or ampicillin/sulbactam alone. Small abscess (<3-4 cm) = antibiotics alone, no drainage needed.
rationale.Cefazolin IV: Complicated diverticulitis: IV cefazolin/cefuroxime/ceftriaxone + metronidazole or ampicillin/sulbactam alone. Small abscess (<3-4 cm) = antibiotics alone, no drainage needed.
rationale.Colonoscopy / Sigmoidoscopy / Barium ene: COLONOSCOPY AND BARIUM ENEMA ARE CONTRAINDICATED in acute diverticulitis — risk of perforation of inflamed bowel.
rationale.Diet, high fiber: High-fiber diet at discharge to prevent further occurrences. Gradually advance from low to high residue.
rationale.Colonoscopy / Barium enema: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in acute diverticulitis. Risk of bowel perforation from inflamed, friable tissue. Colonoscopy only after diverticulitis completely resolves (to rule out malignancy).
rationale.Percutaneous drainage for 2 cm abscess: Abscesses <3-4 cm can be managed with antibiotics alone. Drainage indicated for abscesses >4 cm.

hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with the classic triad of diverticulitis: LLQ pain, low-grade fever, and leukocytosis. He has changes in bowel habits with nausea and vomiting. He meets SIRS criteria (fever >100.4°F, WBC >12,000). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV and oral contrast is the gold standard — findings include bowel wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, and a 2 cm abscess (complicated diverticulitis). Abscesses <3-4 cm can be managed conservatively with antibiotics alone without percutaneous drainage. Colonoscopy and barium enema are CONTRAINDICATED in acute diverticulitis due to risk of perforation. Treatment: NPO for bowel rest, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cefazolin + metronidazole, cefuroxime + metronidazole, ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or ampicillin/sulbactam). High-fiber diet at discharge for prevention.

case_summary: Complicated acute diverticulitis with 2 cm abscess. LLQ pain + fever + leukocytosis (SIRS). CT confirms. NPO + IV fluids + IV ceftriaxone/metronidazole. No drainage needed (<3-4 cm). Avoid colonoscopy. High-fiber diet at discharge.
